nodes.label: BasqueParl
nodes.authors: Escribano, González, Orbegozo-Terradillos, Larrondo-Ureta, Peña-Fernández et al.
nodes.summary: Bilingual Basque-Spanish parliamentary corpus (41k speeches, 14M words, 2012-2020). Headline finding: the chamber president produces 55% of speeches but only 5% of words, so all analyses are reported with and without president texts.
nodes.significance: Bilingual Basque-Spanish parliamentary corpus offering the cleanest published quantification of procedural dominance in turn counts: the chamber president produces 55% of speeches but only 5% of words. It provides direct empirical motivation for filtering or downweighting chair and procedural interventions in per-speaker text measures.
nodes.findings: 41,417 speeches and 13.9M words (2012-2020); the president alone accounts for 55% of speeches, 18% of paragraphs and 5% of words, so analyses are reported with and without president texts. Basque appears in 83.5% of speeches but supplies only 21.2% of words, and women produce 74.5% of speeches but 46.5% of words.
nodes.limitations: No intrinsic accuracy evaluation of any pipeline component (language ID, lemmatization, NER, metadata inference) on the corpus itself; paragraph-level language assignment flattens code-switching, and the analyses are descriptive with no significance testing.

nodes.label: ParlaSent-BCS
nodes.summary: 2,600 sentiment-annotated parliamentary sentences (Bosnia, Croatia, Serbia) with a 6-level reduction-friendly schema; Krippendorff alpha 0.60 (6-class) / 0.745 (ternary) / 0.83 (binary); BERTic beats XLM-R by ~7.6 F1.
nodes.significance: Sentiment-annotated parliamentary sentences from three Balkan parliaments introducing a reduction-friendly 6-level annotation schema and a double-annotation/reconciliation protocol with agreement reported at multiple granularities. It also provides evidence that regional or domain-matched encoders outperform generic multilingual models on parliamentary text.
nodes.findings: Krippendorff's alpha was 0.599 (6-class), 0.745 (ternary) and 0.829 (binary); BERTić reached 0.794 ternary macro-F1, beating XLM-R-base by ~7.6 points, and 0.90 on the binary task. Cross-parliament transfer showed that test-side data difficulty, not training-side origin, drives performance.
nodes.limitations: Only 2,600 sentences with a lexicon-biased, mid-length-only sample; two annotators (both Croatian natives) with half the data single-annotated; Bosnian is severely underrepresented (153 sentences) and the 6-class agreement falls below conventional reliability thresholds.

nodes.label: LLaMandement
nodes.authors: Gesnouin, Tannier, Gomes Da Silva, Tapory, Brier et al.
nodes.summary: French government (DGFiP) LoRA-tuned Llama-2 13B for neutral summarization of legislative amendments; 15,397 amendment-summary pairs released; human eval only (10 drafters, 30 held-out amendments); deployed on the 2024 Finance Bill.
nodes.significance: A deployed French government (DGFiP) system that LoRA-tunes Llama-2 13B for neutral summarization of legislative amendments, releasing 15,397 amendment-summary pairs with institutionally neutral gold targets. It is a rare documented European public-sector LLM deployment on legislative text, combining expert-panel human evaluation with a bias audit against the base model.
nodes.findings: Ten expert drafters rated the fine-tuned 13B at 15.1/20 versus 16.5 for human summaries and 15.5 for few-shot Llama-2 70B, so fine-tuning bought deployment efficiency rather than quality; an auxiliary keyword-based system auto-attributed 94% of ~5,400 amendments on the 2024 Finance Bill.
nodes.limitations: Evaluation used only 30 held-out amendments and 10 raters with no inter-annotator agreement and no automatic metrics, and score standard deviations (±5-7 on a 20-point scale) dwarf the reported gaps; the bias audit was run in English for a French system, and the report is not peer-reviewed.

nodes.label: Knesset-DictaBERT
nodes.summary: MLM-only continued pretraining of DictaBERT on the Hebrew Knesset Corpus (384M tokens): perplexity 22.87 to 6.60, +4.5pp top-1 masked accuracy. No downstream, retrieval, or embedding evaluation at all.
nodes.significance: Applies MLM-only continued pretraining to a Hebrew encoder on the Knesset parliamentary corpus, exemplifying the current state of parliamentary domain-adapted encoders. It also marks a clear gap in the literature: such encoders are evaluated on intrinsic language-modeling metrics but never on retrieval or embedding quality.
nodes.findings: Continued MLM pretraining of DictaBERT on the 384M-token Hebrew Knesset Corpus reduced perplexity from 22.87 to 6.60 and improved top-1 masked-token accuracy by 4.5 percentage points.
nodes.limitations: No downstream, retrieval, or embedding evaluation of any kind; arXiv-only and not peer-reviewed.

nodes.label: ParliaBench
nodes.summary: UK benchmark for conditioned parliamentary speech generation (447k ParlaMint-GB speeches) with novel metrics: embedding-centroid Political Spectrum Alignment, Party Alignment, and Cross-Context Stability = 100/(1+CV). Single 3.8B LLM judge, no human validation.
nodes.significance: Benchmark for conditioned parliamentary speech generation built on 447k ParlaMint-GB speeches, introducing embedding-centroid metrics (Political Spectrum Alignment, Party Alignment) and a Cross-Context Stability meta-metric. One of the first systematic evaluation suites for generated political text.
nodes.findings: Fine-tuning improved Political Spectrum Alignment in all 5 evaluated models (p<0.001, Cohen's d 0.141-1.045) and Party Alignment in 4 of 5 (d 0.099-1.221); ANOVA shows Party Alignment distinguishes parties and PSA distinguishes orientations (both p<0.001).
nodes.limitations: Relies entirely on a single 3.8B LLM judge (Flow-Judge-v0.1) with no human validation; party orientation labels are author-assigned with no external ground truth such as CHES or Manifesto Project data.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: the Cross-Context Stability metric must be attributed to ParliaBench, and the benchmark's lack of external party ground truth and factual grounding marks natural differentiation axes.

nodes.label: PolicyBot
nodes.summary: Policy-document RAG demo: semantic chunking, gte-multilingual embeddings, HyDE + 5x multi-query fused with RRF, bge cross-encoder rerank, local Gemma generation. Citation display only, no verification; components chosen on proxy benchmarks; no end-to-end eval.
nodes.significance: A representative policy-document RAG system combining semantic chunking, multilingual embeddings, HyDE, multi-query expansion fused with RRF, cross-encoder reranking, and local generation. It illustrates the prevailing practice in policy-oriented RAG: stacking fashionable retrieval components chosen on proxy benchmarks, with citations displayed but not verified and no ablation of the stack.
nodes.limitations: Components were selected on proxy benchmarks rather than in-domain evaluation; no end-to-end or ablation study; citations are displayed but not verified; arXiv-only and not peer-reviewed.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG as the closest architectural comparable: it lists citation verification as future work and never ablates its HyDE/multi-query/RRF/reranker stack, motivating measured comparisons against that default recipe.

nodes.label: ParlaCAP
nodes.summary: GPT-4o teacher (~$100 for 35k speeches) trains an XLM-R-Parla student to label ~8M ParlaMint speeches across 28 parliaments with 22 CAP major topics; human-LLM Krippendorff alpha 0.60-0.64 vs inter-human 0.59-0.68; Italian slice is Senate-only and unvalidated.
nodes.significance: Demonstrates a low-cost LLM teacher-student pipeline (~$100 of GPT-4o annotation for ~35k speeches) that labels ~8M ParlaMint speeches across 28 parliaments with 22 CAP major topics via a fine-tuned XLM-R-Parla student. Its human-LLM agreement protocol, requiring human-LLM Krippendorff's alpha to fall within the inter-human range, is a replicable validation recipe for LLM-annotated political text.
nodes.findings: Human-GPT-4o agreement (alpha 0.60-0.64) fell within the inter-human range (0.59-0.68); the fine-tuned student matched the teacher (macro-F1 0.64-0.72 vs 0.63-0.74 across EN/HR/SR/BS) and beat all nine CAP Babel Machine baselines on all four test sets. Targeted augmentation lifted the rare Public Lands class from 0.30 to 0.80 F1.
nodes.limitations: Gold evaluation covers only 4 of 20+ languages, with three of four test sets single-annotated; the Italian slice is Senate-only with unmeasured accuracy, and GPT-4o serves as both teacher and de-facto upper bound, so systematic teacher biases propagate undetected.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: hands over a ready CAP topic layer (label descriptions, prompt, off-the-shelf classifier) plus a replicable teacher-student validation protocol, though Italian gold test data would still need to be built.

nodes.label: Proksch & Slapin 2012
nodes.summary: Canonical comparative theory of legislative speech: floor access is strategically allocated by party rules (electoral system, candidate selection), not a neutral reflection of expertise.
nodes.significance: Canonical comparative theory of legislative speech showing that floor access is strategically allocated by party rules (electoral system, candidate selection, intra-party ideological spread) rather than being a neutral reflection of expertise. It cautions against reading intervention counts as expertise proxies and motivates conditioning speech-based measures on party and institutional role.
nodes.findings: Party rules for debate participation are endogenous to strategic considerations, favoring either leadership control of the floor or backbencher exposure; under strong-party systems, speaking time is allocated top-down.

nodes.label: Politics of Parliamentary Debate (2015)
nodes.summary: Book-length delegation model of speaking time between leaders and backbenchers with cross-national empirics; debate participation tracks party discipline and electoral incentives.
nodes.significance: Book-length delegation model of speaking time between party leaders and backbenchers with cross-national empirics; establishes that debate participation patterns track party discipline and electoral incentives, so speech data must be interpreted through institutional rules.
nodes.findings: Cross-national evidence (Germany, UK, EU, New Zealand) shows debate participation tracks party discipline and electoral incentives, formalized as a delegation game between leaders and backbenchers over speaking time.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: in chambers with group-allocated speaking time (such as the Italian Chamber's contingentamento dei tempi), intervention volume carries party-size and role confounds that per-speaker normalization does not remove.

nodes.label: Back, Debus & Muller 2014
nodes.summary: Swedish Riksdag study: female MPs give fewer speeches, especially in 'hard' policy debates, controlling for seniority and committee assignment.
nodes.significance: Empirical demonstration that parliamentary floor access carries systematic demographic participation biases, so any activity-based measure of speaker importance inherits who gets the floor rather than who knows the topic. Supports demographic sanity checks on speaker-level scores derived from participation.
nodes.findings: In the Swedish Riksdag, female MPs give fewer speeches than male MPs, especially in 'hard' policy debates, controlling for seniority and committee assignment.

nodes.label: Fernandes, Debus & Back 2021
nodes.summary: State-of-the-field review of legislative debate research: what debates are for, who speaks, and under which institutional constraints.
nodes.significance: State-of-the-field review of legislative debate research: what debates are for (position-taking, representation, intra-party signaling), who speaks, and under which institutional constraints. The standard umbrella citation for the claim that speech participation is strategically allocated and cannot be read as raw expertise, motivating multi-signal designs for speaker importance.

nodes.label: Quinn et al. 2010
nodes.summary: Dynamic topic model over US Senate speech establishing per-legislator topic-attention profiles as meaningful quantities; attention tracks committee duties.
nodes.significance: Establishes per-legislator topic-attention profiles as meaningful, measurable quantities via a dynamic topic model over legislative speech; the closest political-science ancestor of topic-conditioned speech measures and support for topic-weighted speech counts over raw counts.
nodes.findings: A dynamic topic model over U.S. Senate floor speech (1997–2004) shows legislators' topic-attention shares track committee duties and agenda events.

nodes.label: Get Out the Vote (2006)
nodes.summary: First influential coupling of floor-speech text with relational structure (agreement links) for vote prediction via collective classification; introduces the ConVote corpus.
nodes.significance: First influential work to couple floor-speech text with relational structure (inter-speaker agreement links) for vote prediction via collective classification, introducing the ConVote corpus. It established that debates are relational objects whose speakers' positions are partly inferable from interaction structure.
nodes.findings: Showed that collective (graph-cut) classification exploiting agreement links between speakers improves support/oppose prediction from US House floor-debate transcripts over classifying speeches in isolation.

nodes.label: Abercrombie & Batista-Navarro survey
nodes.summary: Systematic review of 61 studies on sentiment and position-taking in parliamentary debates, cataloguing preprocessing conventions and the sentiment/stance split.
nodes.significance: Systematic review of 61 studies on sentiment and position-taking analysis in parliamentary debates, cataloguing the field's preprocessing conventions and the split between sentiment and stance framings. It is the standard single entry point for situating new work on opinion measurement in parliamentary text, and documents that procedural filtering is common practice in this literature.
nodes.findings: Catalogues recurring preprocessing choices across 61 studies, including which speeches are excluded and why, and documents the divide between political-science and NLP practice in analyzing parliamentary debates.

nodes.label: HITS (Kleinberg 1999)
nodes.summary: Defines authority as an emergent property of a mutually reinforcing hub-authority link structure computed per query-focused subgraph: authority is topic-conditional.
nodes.significance: Defines authority as an emergent property of a mutually reinforcing hub–authority link structure computed per query-focused subgraph, establishing that authority is topic-conditional rather than a global property. Foundational for all query-conditioned authority and expertise scoring.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: highlights the endorsement dimension (who cites or mentions whom) as a source of authority signal complementary to attribute- and activity-based scoring.

nodes.label: PageRank (Brin & Page 1998)
nodes.summary: Global recursive endorsement-based importance over a link graph; query-independent counterpart to HITS.
nodes.significance: Introduces global recursive endorsement-based importance over a link graph (PageRank), the query-independent counterpart to HITS and the foundational template for prestige priors derived from graph structure.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: a PageRank over mention/citation/co-signature graphs could supply a query-independent prestige prior in place of flat role-based constants.

nodes.label: TREC 2005 Enterprise Track
nodes.summary: Established expert finding as a benchmarked task: rank people by topical expertise, with organizational working-group membership as ground truth.
nodes.significance: Established expert finding as a benchmarked IR task: given a topic, rank people by expertise using documents associated with them, with organizational working-group membership as ground truth. Its evaluation design remains the template for validating people-ranking systems against held-out organizational structure.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: committee membership is the parliamentary analogue of working-group membership as ground truth for validating expert selection.

nodes.label: Balog et al. 2006
nodes.summary: Two generative expert-finding models: candidate-centric (person = their documents) and document-centric (credit people via topic-relevant documents); association strength is the key modeling choice.
nodes.significance: Foundational generative models for expert finding: a candidate-centric model (a person is represented by their documents) and a document-centric model (people are credited via topic-relevant documents), with document–person association strength identified as the key modeling choice.
nodes.findings: Two generative expert-finding models (candidate-centric Model 1 and document-centric Model 2) were formalized and evaluated on the W3C enterprise corpus; the strength of document–person association emerged as the crucial modeling choice.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: the document-centric model suggests scoring authority from the retrieved evidence pool itself, and graded association strengths justify weighting primary versus co-signatures differently.

nodes.label: Expertise Retrieval survey (2012)
nodes.authors: Balog, Fang, de Rijke, Serdyukov & Si
nodes.summary: Comprehensive survey grouping expertise-retrieval approaches into five families and covering evidence beyond documents: position, social ties, temporal dynamics.
nodes.significance: Comprehensive survey of expertise retrieval that groups approaches into five families (profile-centric, document-centric, graph-based, voting/fusion, discriminative) and covers evidence beyond documents: organizational position, social ties, and temporal dynamics. The standard citation for framing linear weighted combinations of heterogeneous expertise evidence as an established voting/fusion design.

nodes.label: Author-Topic Model (2004)
nodes.summary: Each author is a learned distribution over topics from their documents, enabling who-writes-about-what queries.
nodes.significance: The author-topic model represents each author as a learned distribution over topics inferred from their documents, enabling who-writes-about-what queries and author similarity. Probabilistic ancestor of per-speaker topical profiles, suggesting precomputed per-person topic distributions as a cheaper alternative to per-query scoring.

nodes.label: Expertise Networks (Zhang et al. 2007)
nodes.summary: ExpertiseRank (PageRank variant) versus simple measures on the Java Forum: graph-recursive algorithms did not beat simple degree-style counts; performance depends on network structure.
nodes.significance: Benchmarks graph-recursive authority algorithms against simple measures on an online expertise network, showing that structural sophistication must be validated rather than presumed: the performance of authority algorithms depends on network structure.
nodes.findings: On the Java Forum who-helps-whom network, ExpertiseRank (a PageRank variant) and HITS did not outperform simple degree-style measures such as answer count.

nodes.label: TwitterRank (2010)
nodes.summary: Topic-sensitive PageRank with transition probabilities weighted by content similarity between users; influence is computed per topic and beats global PageRank.
nodes.significance: Clearest published precedent for topic-conditional influence: a topic-sensitive PageRank whose transition probabilities are weighted by content similarity between users, combining graph structure with content. Establishes that influence should be computed per topic rather than globally.
nodes.findings: Per-topic influence computed with content-similarity-weighted transitions outperformed both global PageRank and topic-sensitive PageRank baselines on Twitter data.

nodes.label: Connecting the Congress (Fowler 2006)
nodes.summary: Cosponsorship networks from ~280k US bills; 'connectedness' centrality weighting cosponsorship predicts legislative influence outcomes.
nodes.significance: Foundational study of legislative cosponsorship networks: defines a closeness-flavored 'connectedness' centrality weighting cosponsorship frequency and bill cosponsor counts, and validates network position as a predictor of legislative influence. Legitimizes signature graphs as authority evidence in legislatures.
nodes.findings: From roughly 280,000 U.S. bills (1973–2004), connectedness centrality in the cosponsorship network predicts legislative influence outcomes such as amendment success.

nodes.label: House committee networks (2005)
nodes.summary: Committee-committee networks via membership interlocks in the US House recover hierarchical and political structure from membership alone.
nodes.significance: Shows that committee membership encodes real political and topical structure: committee–committee networks built from membership interlocks alone recover the hierarchical and political organization of a legislature.
nodes.findings: In the U.S. House, networks of committees connected by membership interlocks recover hierarchical structure and political correlations without using any text or voting data beyond membership (plus roll-call SVD checks).

nodes.label: Italian Chamber voting network (2014)
nodes.authors: Dal Maso, Pompa, Puliga, Riotta & Chessa
nodes.summary: Co-voting similarity network over deputies of the Italian Chamber of Deputies; community detection recovers coalitions and quantifies cohesion and government strength.
nodes.significance: Demonstrates that deputy-level network analysis over roll-call votes recovers meaningful political structure in the Italian Chamber of Deputies: co-voting similarity networks support community detection of coalitions and topological quantification of party cohesion and government strength.
nodes.findings: Community detection on the co-voting similarity network of Italian Chamber deputies recovers governing coalitions, and topological metrics quantify party cohesion and government strength over time.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: proof that large-scale individual voting records in this exact chamber support deputy-level network analysis, grounding coalition-period filtering logic.

nodes.label: Card et al. 2022 (procedural classifier)
nodes.authors: Card, Chang, Becker, Mendelsohn, Voigt et al.
nodes.summary: 140-year Congressional Record study that trains classifiers to identify and exclude procedural speeches (rules, vote announcements, turn management) before substantive analysis.
nodes.significance: A 140-year computational study of the US Congressional Record that trains supervised classifiers to identify and exclude procedural speeches (rules, vote announcements, turn management) before substantive analysis. It supplies the canonical citable methodology for procedural filtering in large-scale legislative text analysis.
nodes.findings: Found that the framing of immigration in US political speech became more positive but increasingly polarized over 140 years; methodologically, procedural speeches were classified and removed before any substantive text measure was computed.

nodes.label: Aroyehun et al. 2025
nodes.authors: Aroyehun, Simchon, Carrella, Lasser, Lewandowsky & Garcia
nodes.summary: Nature Human Behaviour study over ~8M congressional speeches; removes procedural speeches with a majority-vote ensemble of three classifiers following Card et al. before any text measure.
nodes.significance: Top-venue (Nature Human Behaviour) analysis of ~8M US congressional speeches documenting a long-run shift from evidence-based to intuition-based language. Its preprocessing, which removes procedural speeches with a majority-vote ensemble of three classifiers following Card et al., is the strongest recent precedent that procedural filtering is required hygiene before per-speaker text aggregates.
nodes.findings: Over ~8M congressional speeches, the analysis reveals a shift from evidence-based to intuition-based language; procedural speeches were removed via a majority-vote ensemble of three classifiers before computing any text measure.

nodes.label: Aroyehun et al. 2026 (preprint)
nodes.summary: 15M speech segments across 7 countries (1946-2025); chair-speech removal and LLM-rated procedural filtering feed an Evidence-Minus-Intuition score.
nodes.significance: Preprint scaling epistemic-orientation measurement to 15M speech segments across seven countries (1946-2025), computing an Evidence-Minus-Intuition score after chair-speech removal and LLM-rated procedural filtering. It represents current frontier practice of applying procedural filtering before any per-speaker aggregate in cross-national parliamentary analysis.
nodes.findings: Reports that epistemic orientation in parliamentary discourse is associated with deliberative-democracy indicators, computed over 15M speech segments from 7 countries (1946-2025) after chair removal and procedural filtering.
nodes.limitations: arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed; the source report could not confirm which paper in this cluster contains the specific LLM procedural-rating rule (0-4 scale, exclude >2), so that detail requires verification against the PDF.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: an index-time LLM procedural rating is the lowest-engineering-cost procedural-filtering option for a stack that already includes an LLM annotation pass.

nodes.label: Mining Ethos (Duthie et al. 2016)
nodes.summary: Annotates and automatically recognizes ethotic expressions (support/attack on a speaker's character) in Hansard, with polarity.
nodes.significance: Introduces ethos mining: annotating and automatically recognizing ethotic expressions (support or attack on a speaker's character) in parliamentary debate, with polarity. Ethos mining yields a text-derived endorsement graph capturing reputation among peers, a dimension absent from activity- and attribute-based authority measures.
nodes.findings: Ethotic support/attack expressions in UK Hansard were annotated with polarity and recognized automatically, demonstrating feasibility of mining character-directed endorsement from floor debate text.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: an ethos-mined endorsement network over speaker-mention edges would add a reputation-among-peers component to authority scoring.

nodes.label: Krehbiel 1991
nodes.summary: The informational theory of legislative organization: committees exist so legislators specialize and acquire policy expertise the chamber then exploits.
nodes.significance: The informational theory of legislative organization: committees exist so that legislators specialize and acquire policy expertise which the chamber then exploits, with composition and procedure designed to incentivize truthful transmission of that expertise. The discipline's core theoretical justification for treating committee membership as an expertise signal.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: provides the theoretical grounding for committee-membership components and committee-officer bonuses in speaker authority scoring.

nodes.label: Legislative Effectiveness (2014)
nodes.summary: Defines the Legislative Effectiveness Score: a per-legislator composite over bill-progression stages times significance tiers, normalized per Congress.
nodes.significance: Defines the Legislative Effectiveness Score (LES), the closest existing validated composite per-legislator score: a composite over bill-progression stages times significance tiers, normalized per Congress. Establishes outcome-weighted legislative activity as a validated measurement practice and a natural external validation target for other legislator-level scores.
nodes.findings: The LES combines 15 indicators (5 bill-progression stages × 3 significance tiers) per legislator per Congress; member attributes such as seniority, committee chair positions, and majority status predict effectiveness.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: adding act-outcome progression stages to activity-based components, and using an LES-style score as an external validation target, follow directly from this design.

nodes.label: T-Rank (2005)
nodes.summary: Extends PageRank with temporal freshness and activity of pages and links; authority flows preferentially through fresh, active edges.
nodes.significance: Direct precedent for injecting time into authority computation: extends PageRank with temporal freshness and activity of pages and links so that authority flows preferentially through fresh, active edges. Its freshness/activity split suggests distinguishing recent activity from long-run specialization, which a single decay half-life conflates.

nodes.label: Temporal Expertise Profiling (2014)
nodes.summary: Models a person's expertise as a time series of hierarchical topic-profile snapshots with change detection.
nodes.significance: Models a person's expertise as a time series of hierarchical topic-profile snapshots with change detection, validating date-parameterized expertise scoring and time-sliced profiles, and suggesting per-person expertise trajectories as a consistency check.

nodes.label: Echoes of Power (2012)
nodes.summary: Power differentials are detectable from linguistic coordination: lower-power participants echo the function-word style of higher-power ones (Wikipedia, US Supreme Court).
nodes.significance: Shows power differentials are detectable from purely linguistic signals: lower-power participants echo the function-word style of higher-power ones. Offers a text-derived, activity-independent power measure useful for externally validating authority scores against real standing rather than volume.
nodes.findings: Linguistic coordination asymmetries track power differentials on Wikipedia discussions and U.S. Supreme Court oral arguments, distinguishing status power from situational dependence.

nodes.label: AIS (Rashkin et al. 2023)
nodes.summary: Defines Attributable to Identified Sources: output y is attributable to source P iff a generic hearer would affirm 'According to P, y'; two-stage human protocol with an interpretability step.
nodes.significance: Defines Attributable to Identified Sources (AIS): an output y is attributable to source P iff a generic hearer would affirm 'According to P, y', operationalized as a two-stage human protocol. It is the foundational conceptual framework for measuring attribution in natural language generation.
nodes.findings: The two-stage protocol (an interpretability step followed by a binary AIS judgment) was validated on conversational QA, summarization, and table-to-text; the framework explicitly excludes world knowledge, so only the identified source counts.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: a literal-substring check on quote spans is a deterministic sufficient condition for AIS, while AIS itself delimits what such a check does not cover (the surrounding prose).

nodes.label: Attributed QA / AutoAIS
nodes.summary: Formulates attributed QA and proposes AutoAIS: an NLI model predicting whether the cited passage entails the answer, correlating with human AIS at system level (~0.96 reported).
nodes.significance: Formulates the attributed QA task (question to answer-plus-attribution-passage) and introduces AutoAIS, an NLI model predicting whether the cited passage entails the answer, establishing NLI entailment as the standard automatic proxy for human attribution judgments.
nodes.findings: AutoAIS (a fine-tuned T5 NLI model) correlates with human AIS judgments at system level (~0.96 reported); the paper benchmarks retrieve-then-read, post-hoc-retrieval, and LLM-plus-rerank architectures on Natural Questions.
nodes.limitations: Released as an arXiv report without a peer-reviewed venue; the AutoAIS correlation with human judgment is established at system level rather than per instance.

nodes.label: Attribution/Citation/Quotation survey
nodes.summary: Systematizes 134 papers and ~300 metrics; separates citation (marker), attribution (output-evidence link), and quotation (verbatim reuse); only 13% of papers quote at all.
nodes.significance: Systematizes 134 papers and ~300 metrics on evidence-based text generation, cleanly separating citation (marker to source), attribution (output-evidence link), and quotation (verbatim reuse). It provides the field map showing how rarely these paradigms are combined.
nodes.findings: Across the surveyed literature roughly 75% of papers cite, 62% attribute, and only 13% quote, making quotation the rarest paradigm and the intersection of all three nearly empty.

nodes.label: WebGPT
nodes.summary: GPT-3 fine-tuned to browse with an explicit quote action clipping verbatim extracts into a reference buffer; answers cite references by index; RLHF-trained.
nodes.significance: Early browser-assisted question answering: GPT-3 is fine-tuned to drive a text browser with an explicit quote action that clips verbatim extracts into a reference buffer, then composes answers that cite those references by index. It established the collect-then-cite pattern for grounded generation.
nodes.findings: Trained with behavioral cloning and RLHF, with humans judging factual support; the quote action guarantees the reference pool itself is verbatim corpus text.
nodes.limitations: Only the reference pool is guaranteed verbatim; fidelity of the final answer to those references is encouraged by RLHF rather than verified.

nodes.label: GopherCite
nodes.summary: 280B model trained (SFT + RLHF) to answer with claim + source + quoted passage; Supported & Plausible 80% (NQ) / 67% (ELI5), human-verified; verbatimness is a trained tendency, not a guarantee.
nodes.significance: A 280B Gopher-based model trained (SFT plus RLHF with reward-model reranking) to answer with claim, source, and quoted passage, making verbatim quoting a learned behavior. It is the canonical quote-generating system against which enforced-quoting approaches are contrasted.
nodes.findings: Supported & Plausible (human protocol) reaches 80% on a NaturalQuestions subset and 67% on ELI5; the paper itself shows S&P answers can still be false.
nodes.limitations: Verbatimness is a trained tendency enforced by syntax and learning signal, not a hard constraint; verification is fundamentally human, and the work appeared only as a tech report.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: the sharpest published contrast between learned quoting verified by humans at 67-80% and a deterministic substring post-condition.

nodes.label: 'According to...' / QUIP-Score
nodes.authors: Weller, Marone, Weir, Lawrie, Khashabi & Van Durme
nodes.summary: Grounding phrases increase verbatim overlap with a trusted corpus; QUIP-Score measures character n-gram membership via a Bloom-filter index; higher QUIP correlates with fewer hallucinations.
nodes.significance: Shows that grounding phrases ('According to ...') increase verbatim overlap with a trusted corpus, and introduces QUIP-Score, which measures grounding as character n-gram membership in the corpus via a Bloom-filter index rather than via NLI.
nodes.findings: Grounding prompts increase verbatim quoting from pre-training data, demonstrated on Wikipedia, PubMed, and the US tax code; higher QUIP-Score correlates with fewer hallucinations.

nodes.label: Quote-Tuning
nodes.authors: Zhang, Marone, Li, Van Durme & Khashabi
nodes.summary: DPO alignment toward verbatim quoting scored by Bloom-filter corpus membership: up to ~130% relative quoting increase with maintained quality; 'verifiable by design' thesis.
nodes.significance: Aligns language models toward verbatim quoting via DPO, using fast Bloom-filter corpus-membership scoring to build preference pairs. It is the strongest peer-reviewed articulation of the 'verifiable by design' thesis: verbatim quotation as a verifiability feature achieved through training.
nodes.findings: Achieves up to ~130% relative increase in verbatim quoting while maintaining response quality.
nodes.limitations: Verification is n-gram membership over a corpus sketch, not contiguous-substring verification against a single identified source document; quoting remains a trained tendency rather than a guarantee.

nodes.label: NEST (speculative span splicing)
nodes.summary: Token-level kNN retrieval with speculative acceptance of retrieved corpus spans; accepted spans are real corpus text so span-level attribution comes free; 1.8x speedup.
nodes.significance: Nearest Neighbor Speculative Decoding: token-level kNN retrieval forms a semi-parametric mixture, and a speculative procedure accepts prefixes of retrieved corpus spans or falls back to model tokens. Accepted spans are real corpus text, so span-level attribution comes for free at decoding time.
nodes.findings: Provides span-level attribution as a by-product of decoding and a 1.8x speedup on Llama-2-Chat 70B.
nodes.limitations: Copying is probabilistic and interleaved, so the output is a mosaic of spliced spans without explicit, reader-visible quote boundaries.

nodes.label: Attribute First, then Generate
nodes.summary: Decomposes generation into span selection, sentence planning, and per-sentence fusion of only the selected spans, giving span-level attribution by construction.
nodes.significance: Decomposes grounded generation into content selection (span picking), sentence planning, and per-sentence fusion of only the selected spans, so each output sentence carries the exact source spans it was fused from. This yields span-level attribution by construction rather than by post-hoc alignment.
nodes.findings: Demonstrates locally-attributable generation where attribution requires no post-hoc alignment step, since provenance is fixed during planning.
nodes.limitations: Output sentences are still abstractive fusions of the selected spans, so fidelity to those spans remains model-dependent rather than verbatim.

nodes.label: ReClaim
nodes.summary: Interleaves verbatim reference spans with claim sentences; reports ~90% citation accuracy, measured, not guaranteed.
nodes.significance: Interleaves verbatim reference spans with claim sentences during retrieval-augmented generation, grounding every sentence in an explicit quoted reference. It exemplifies quote-then-claim interleaving where citation accuracy is measured rather than enforced.
nodes.findings: Reports ~90% citation accuracy.
nodes.limitations: Citation accuracy is measured, not guaranteed; no deterministic gate strips quotes that fail verification.

nodes.label: VeriCite
nodes.summary: Per-claim NLI verification during generation, evidence selection, then LLM refinement rewriting the answer with verified citations; all verification is semantic, no substring guarantee.
nodes.significance: A state-of-the-art NLI-side citation pipeline: per-claim NLI verification against retrieved passages during generation, supporting-evidence selection, and LLM refinement that rewrites the answer with verified citations. It represents rigorous semantic (claim-level) verification within the generation loop.
nodes.findings: Combines three stages (per-claim NLI verification, evidence selection, LLM refinement) to improve citation reliability in RAG.
nodes.limitations: All verification is semantic (NLI/similarity) with no substring guarantee, and the refinement step is itself an LLM, so guarantees remain probabilistic.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: a natural head-to-head baseline, since NLI pipelines verify claims but not quotes, while verbatim-quote systems verify quotes but not claims.

nodes.label: FRONT
nodes.summary: Grounds outputs in fine-grained supporting quotes before generating; improves ALCE citation quality by ~14% on LLaMA-2-7B, surpassing ChatGPT.
nodes.significance: FRONT first grounds outputs in fine-grained supporting quotes extracted from retrieved documents, then generates conditioned on those quotes. It provides direct published evidence that quote-first grounding improves NLI-measured citation quality.
nodes.findings: On the ALCE benchmark, LLaMA-2-7B with FRONT improves citation quality by an average of 14.21%, surpassing ChatGPT.
nodes.limitations: Evaluation still relies on ALCE's NLI metrics, underscoring that quote grounding and entailment evaluation are complements rather than substitutes.

nodes.label: ALCE
nodes.summary: The canonical citation-evaluation benchmark: NLI-based citation recall (cited passages entail the statement) and precision (leave-one-out irrelevance test); best models lack complete support ~50% of the time on ELI5.
nodes.significance: The canonical benchmark for citation evaluation: NLI-judged citation recall (cited passages must entail the statement) and citation precision (leave-one-out irrelevance test), judged by the TRUE model (T5-11B fine-tuned on NLI collections). It defines the reference vocabulary for measuring whether prose statements are supported by their citations.
nodes.findings: Best models lack complete citation support roughly 50% of the time on ELI5; the automatic metrics correlate strongly with human judgment.
nodes.limitations: Verdicts come from a probabilistic NLI judge and measure semantic support of statements, not verbatimness, quote authenticity, or speaker identity.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: verbatim quote-fidelity metrics do not measure ALCE-style prose-statement support, so the two families of metrics need to be reported side by side.

nodes.label: RARR
nodes.summary: Post-hoc research-and-revise: retrieve evidence for any generator's output, minimally edit unsupported content, emit an attribution report; measures attribution-preservation trade-off.
nodes.significance: The archetype of post-hoc attribution and revision: take any generator's output, retrieve evidence via generated search queries, minimally edit unsupported content while preserving intent, and emit an attribution report. It frames the design axis of revising after generation versus constraining during generation.
nodes.findings: Introduces and measures the attribution-versus-preservation trade-off (AIS-based) for post-hoc revision of arbitrary model outputs.

nodes.label: L-CiteEval
nodes.authors: Tang, Zhou, Li, Ji, Hou & Zhang
nodes.summary: Long-context citation benchmark (8K-48K): citation fidelity degrades with context length; open models trail closed ones, suggesting parametric answering over context grounding.
nodes.significance: A fully automated long-context citation benchmark (11 tasks, 8K-48K token contexts) scoring answer quality and citation recall/precision over context chunks. It shows that citation fidelity is a function of context length, which matters for any system operating over long source documents.
nodes.findings: Citation fidelity degrades as context length grows; open long-context models trail closed ones badly on citation quality, suggesting they answer from parametric knowledge rather than grounding in the context; citations are correlated with attention patterns.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: parliamentary sessions are long documents, motivating reporting citation metrics as a function of retrieved-context size.

nodes.label: Verifiability of generative search engines
nodes.summary: Human audit of Bing Chat, NeevaAI, perplexity.ai, YouChat: only 51.5% of sentences fully supported by citations, 74.5% citation precision; fluency inversely correlates with citation quality.
nodes.significance: Human audit of deployed generative search engines (Bing Chat, NeevaAI, perplexity.ai, YouChat) that established citation recall and citation precision as human-judged measures for real systems. It documented the 'fluent but unsupported' failure mode of deployed citing systems.
nodes.findings: On average only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations, with 74.5% citation precision; fluency and perceived utility inversely correlate with citation quality.

nodes.label: Correctness is not Faithfulness
nodes.summary: Splits citation correctness (cited document entails statement) from citation faithfulness (the model causally relied on it); up to ~57% of citations lack faithfulness even when correct.
nodes.significance: Splits citation correctness (the cited document entails the statement, as ALCE/TRUE measure) from citation faithfulness (the model causally relied on the cited document rather than post-rationalizing citations onto parametric answers). This adds a third axis to attribution evaluation beyond authenticity and semantic support.
nodes.findings: Up to ~57% of citations lack faithfulness even when they are correct.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: verbatim quotes prove correctness of the quoted material by construction but say nothing about causal reliance or support of the surrounding claims.

nodes.label: AttrScore
nodes.authors: Yue, Wang, Chen, Zhang, Su & Sun
nodes.summary: Replaces binary entailment with a 3-way attributable / extrapolatory / contradictory scheme for finer attribution error identification.
nodes.significance: Replaces binary entailment with a 3-way attributable / extrapolatory / contradictory scheme for automatic attribution evaluation, enabling finer error identification. The extrapolatory category captures unsupported interpretation of genuine evidence, a dominant failure mode in political and opinionated text.
nodes.findings: Evaluates prompted LLM judges and fine-tuned small models on data repurposed from QA, fact-checking, NLI, and summarization, showing the 3-way scheme identifies attribution errors that binary entailment conflates.

nodes.label: AttributionBench
nodes.summary: Unifies attribution datasets; even fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reaches only ~80% macro-F1 on binary attributability.
nodes.significance: A meta-evaluation that unifies attribution datasets to measure how reliable automatic attribution judges themselves are. It quantifies the ceiling on NLI/LLM-based attribution evaluation, which any verification pipeline built on such judges inherits.
nodes.findings: Even fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reaches only ~80% macro-F1 on binary attributability; error analysis points to insensitivity to fine-grained information and human-model information mismatch.

nodes.label: Fabricated references study
nodes.summary: 636 ChatGPT-generated citations audited: 55% of GPT-3.5 references fabricated versus 18% for GPT-4; many real ones contain substantive errors.
nodes.significance: Peer-reviewed audit quantifying fabricated bibliographic references in LLM output, the standard empirical motivation for retrieval-grounded citation construction over model-recalled references.
nodes.findings: Of 636 citations from 84 short literature reviews, 55% of GPT-3.5 references were fabricated versus 18% for GPT-4; among real references, 43% versus 24% contained substantive errors.

nodes.label: Hallucination snowballing
nodes.summary: LMs over-commit to early mistakes and generate further false claims they can separately recognize as wrong (self-recognition 67-94%).
nodes.significance: Documents hallucination snowballing: language models over-commit to early mistakes and generate further false claims that they can separately recognize as wrong. It motivates per-statement verification, since a single unsupported claim can propagate through subsequent generation.
nodes.findings: Self-recognition of the snowballed false claims ranges from 67% to 94% across GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and LLaMA2-70B-chat, and the effect persists across decoding strategies.

nodes.label: LLM hallucination survey (TOIS)
nodes.summary: LLM-era canonical survey: factuality versus faithfulness hallucination, causes across data/training/inference, and RAG-specific 'context-inconsistency'.
nodes.significance: The LLM-era canonical hallucination survey: distinguishes factuality from faithfulness hallucination, maps causes across data, training, and inference, and names the RAG-specific failure of 'context-inconsistency' where generation departs from retrieved context. It supplies the standard taxonomy for scoping what any faithfulness guarantee does and does not cover.

nodes.label: SummaC
nodes.summary: NLI entailment matrix over document x summary sentences; granularity fix lifts NLI inconsistency detection to 72-74% balanced accuracy; thresholds require per-dataset calibration.
nodes.significance: Shows that earlier NLI-based inconsistency detection failed due to a granularity mismatch, and fixes it with an M x N entailment matrix over document sentences by summary sentences with max-then-mean aggregation. The max-scoring premise also identifies which source sentence supports each generated sentence, enabling automatic evidence binding.
nodes.findings: SummaC-ZS reaches 72.1% balanced accuracy and SummaC-Conv 74.4% (+5 points over prior SOTA) on inconsistency detection; the best NLI training mix was MNLI plus Vitamin-C.
nodes.limitations: Binary decision thresholds are tuned per dataset, so deployment requires calibration; the NLI backbones are English-trained.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: retrieved chunk sentences as premises and each prose sentence as hypothesis, with max-aggregation identifying the supporting chunk for automatic sentence-level citation binding.

nodes.label: QAFactEval
nodes.summary: Component-optimized QA-based factual-consistency pipeline reaching 77.8% balanced accuracy; shows QA and NLI signals are complementary.
nodes.significance: A component-optimized QA-based factual-consistency pipeline (NP-chunk answer selection, BART-large question generation, Electra-large QA, answerability filtering, LERC answer-overlap scoring). Its key result is that QA-based and NLI-based consistency signals are complementary, motivating layered verification.
nodes.findings: Reaches 77.8% balanced accuracy on the SummaC benchmark, ~14% over prior QA metrics and above the best entailment metric; combining QA and NLI signals improves further.
nodes.limitations: All pipeline components are English-trained, so porting to another language requires new question-generation and QA models.

nodes.label: FActScore
nodes.summary: Decomposes long-form generations into atomic facts (LLM-drafted; humans revised ~52% of them) verified against retrieved passages; score = fraction supported.
nodes.significance: Decomposes long-form generations into atomic facts verified individually against retrieved passages, with the score being the fraction supported. Per-claim verification is more diagnostic than per-sentence scoring for prose that packs multiple claims into single sentences.
nodes.findings: Human annotators revised ~52% of the LLM-drafted atomic facts (18% splits, 34% merges), showing decomposition is genuinely hard; the best automatic estimator comes within 2% of human annotation on biographies.
nodes.limitations: The atomic-fact decomposer itself is unreliable (~52% human revision rate), so it needs validation before its verdicts can be trusted.

nodes.label: AlignScore
nodes.summary: Single 355M alignment function trained on 4.7M examples from 7 task families; matches or beats ChatGPT/GPT-4 judges on 22 factual-consistency datasets.
nodes.significance: A single 355M-parameter RoBERTa alignment function trained on 4.7M examples from 7 task families (NLI, QA, paraphrase, fact verification, IR, STS, summarization), scoring chunked context against claim sentences. It demonstrates that a small self-hosted model can match large LLM judges for factual-consistency evaluation.
nodes.findings: The 355M model matches or beats ChatGPT/GPT-4 judges on 22 factual-consistency datasets, using ~350-token context chunking with max-over-chunks and mean-over-sentences aggregation.
nodes.limitations: English-trained; use in other languages requires a multilingual retrain or a translation step.

nodes.label: Self-RAG
nodes.summary: Fine-tunes an LM to emit reflection tokens including ISSUP (segment fully/partially/not supported by passage), enabling decoding-time faithfulness control.
nodes.significance: Fine-tunes an LM to emit reflection tokens — Retrieve, ISREL (passage relevance), ISSUP (segment fully/partially/not supported), and ISUSE (utility) — making retrieval and faithfulness controllable at decoding time via segment-level beam search. The ISSUP label schema is a reusable design for per-segment support checking.
nodes.findings: Llama-2 7B/13B models trained with critic labels distilled from GPT-4 can dial faithfulness at decoding time by re-ranking segments on weighted reflection-token probabilities.
nodes.limitations: Requires a custom fine-tuned model to emit the reflection tokens, so the mechanism is not available to off-the-shelf generators.

nodes.label: Chain-of-Verification
nodes.summary: Draft, plan verification questions, answer them independently (withholding the draft to avoid sycophancy), then revise; factored variants win.
nodes.significance: Chain-of-Verification: draft an answer, plan verification questions, answer them independently, then revise. Its key methodological lesson is that factored variants which withhold the draft during verification avoid sycophantic agreement, a principle applicable to any LLM-judge configuration.
nodes.findings: Factored variants that answer verification questions without seeing the original draft outperform joint variants at reducing hallucination.
nodes.limitations: Prompting-only: verification relies on additional LLM calls with no trained verifier, so verdicts inherit the judge's own error rate.

nodes.label: RAGAS
nodes.summary: Reference-free LLM-judged RAG metrics (faithfulness by statement decomposition, answer and context relevance); the paper's entire human validation is 50 synthetic Wikipedia items.
nodes.significance: Widely adopted reference-free framework for LLM-judged RAG evaluation, decomposing answers into statements for faithfulness checking alongside answer relevance and context relevance. It largely defined the default automated RAG evaluation stack.
nodes.findings: On WikiEval (50 synthetic Wikipedia items, 2 annotators), pairwise-preference accuracy against humans was 0.95 for faithfulness, 0.78 for answer relevance, and 0.70 for context relevance.
nodes.limitations: Human validation is limited to 50 synthetic English Wikipedia items in a demo-track paper; scores inherit LLM-judge noise and are unvalidated outside that setting.

nodes.label: Why Language Models Hallucinate
nodes.summary: Statistical account: hallucinations are ordinary errors of an implicit valid/invalid classifier, and post-training worsens them because benchmarks reward confident guessing.
nodes.significance: A statistical account of hallucination: hallucinations are ordinary errors of an implicit valid/invalid classifier, bounded by the singleton-fact rate, and post-training worsens them because benchmarks reward confident guessing over abstention. It argues model-level elimination is unavailable, motivating system-level guarantees instead.
nodes.findings: Derives that hallucination rates are lower-bounded by properties of the training distribution (singleton facts) and shows standard benchmark incentives push post-trained models toward confident guessing.
nodes.limitations: arXiv preprint; the account is theoretical rather than an empirical benchmark result.

nodes.label: Pointer-Generator Networks
nodes.summary: Per-step soft interpolation between vocabulary generation and copying source tokens via attention; copying is probabilistic, with no phrase-level verbatim guarantee.
nodes.significance: The canonical soft copy mechanism: a per-step generation probability interpolates between vocabulary sampling and copying a source token via attention, with a coverage mechanism curbing repetition. It is the ancestor of all later copy-oriented approaches to faithful text reuse.
nodes.findings: Explicitly motivated by accurate reproduction of source information in abstractive summarization; copying remains per-token and probabilistic.
nodes.limitations: Copying is per-token and probabilistic, so it provides no phrase-level verbatim guarantee.

nodes.label: SEAL (autoregressive search)
nodes.authors: Bevilacqua, Ottaviano, Lewis, Yih, Riedel & Petroni
nodes.summary: BART + FM-index constrained decoding: only continuations that exist verbatim in the corpus can be emitted, so generated n-grams are guaranteed attested substrings; ~10 points over retrievers on KILT.
nodes.significance: BART with an FM-index over the entire corpus: at each decoding step the index masks the vocabulary so only continuations that exist verbatim in the corpus can be emitted, guaranteeing generated n-grams are attested substrings mapped back to passages. It proves corpus-scale exact-substring-constrained decoding is feasible.
nodes.findings: Improves ~10 points over established retrievers on KILT, scoring generated substrings by LM probability times corpus frequency.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: generation-time substring-constrained decoding is the dual of post-hoc quote verification and a candidate path for local deployment.

nodes.label: CAMS (claim-anchored provenance)
nodes.summary: Multi-document summarization with provenance resolved deterministically from verbatim quotes to token spans; faithfulness of surrounding text is encouraged, not NLI-gated; no metadata graph.
nodes.significance: Claim-anchored multi-document summarization where provenance is resolved deterministically from verbatim quotes to token spans (exact substring first, Levenshtein fallback), explicitly distinguishing provenance-as-invariant from faithfulness-as-objective. It is among the closest published hybrids of deterministic verbatim provenance and abstractive generation.
nodes.findings: Resolves quote provenance deterministically to token spans while faithfulness of the surrounding text is encouraged through constrained rewriting.
nodes.limitations: Faithfulness of surrounding text is only encouraged, not NLI-gated; there is no speaker/metadata graph; arXiv preprint.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: the nearest published hybrid — deterministic verbatim provenance without entailment gating or a metadata graph — and thus a key comparison point for novelty claims.

nodes.label: Speaker attribution in Bundestag debates
nodes.summary: GePaDe_SpkAtt: 7,700+ annotated speech/thought/writing events in Bundestag debates with source/addressee/message roles; attribution treated as a learned prediction problem.
nodes.significance: GePaDe_SpkAtt: a corpus of 7,700+ annotated speech, thought, and writing events in Bundestag debates with source, addressee, and message roles, treating speaker attribution as a learned prediction problem. It shows that who-said-what within an utterance (reported speech) is nontrivial even in parliamentary records where the primary speaker is known.
nodes.findings: Provides baselines for trigger detection and role classification over 7,700+ annotated events in German parliamentary debates.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: reported speech inside utterances is the residual attribution error mode even when first-order speaker attribution is structural, motivating detection of nested third-party quotes.

nodes.label: Towards Fair RAG (Kim & Diaz)
nodes.summary: First systematic evaluation of RAG with exposure-fair stochastic retrievers across 12 models / 7 tasks; distinguishes ranking fairness from attribution fairness (exposure of sources actually cited); fair retrieval often maintains or improves quality.
nodes.significance: Central reference on fairness in retrieval-augmented generation: first systematic evaluation of RAG with exposure-fair stochastic retrievers, distinguishing ranking fairness (exposure of retrieved items) from attribution fairness (exposure of sources actually cited in the answer). Shows fair retrieval need not cost generation quality.
nodes.findings: Across 12 RAG models and 7 tasks, fairness-aware (stochastic, exposure-fair) retrieval often maintains or improves both ranking quality and generation quality, and yields more balanced citation attribution.

nodes.label: ARES
nodes.summary: Synthetic-data-fine-tuned lightweight RAG judges anchored by prediction-powered inference on a small human-labeled set, yielding statistically corrected confidence intervals.
nodes.significance: Formalizes cheap automatic RAG judging anchored by prediction-powered inference: synthetic-data-fine-tuned lightweight judges are statistically corrected with a small human-labeled set, yielding confidence intervals with honest coverage. A key methodological template for combining automatic evaluators with limited expert annotation.
nodes.findings: Fine-tuned lightweight judges combined with PPI over a few hundred human labels were shown accurate under domain shift across 8 KILT/SuperGLUE/AIS tasks.
nodes.limitations: Requires a human-annotated anchor set on the order of a few hundred labels; smaller anchors produce wide confidence intervals.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: a small existing set of expert pairwise judgments can serve directly as the PPI anchor, though sets below the recommended few hundred labels yield wide confidence intervals.

nodes.label: RGB benchmark
nodes.summary: Benchmarks four RAG abilities with largely deterministic scoring: noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness; LLMs struggle at rejection and integration.
nodes.significance: Benchmarks four RAG abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) with largely deterministic scoring, demonstrating that meaningful RAG failure modes are measurable without an LLM judge.
nodes.findings: LLMs struggle badly at negative rejection (refusing to answer when the context lacks the answer) and at information integration.

nodes.label: CRAG benchmark (Meta)
nodes.summary: 4,409 QA pairs, 5 domains, mock web + KG search APIs; correct/missing/hallucinated scoring; SOTA industry RAG at most 63% hallucination-free, worst on dynamic facts and tail entities.
nodes.significance: Large-scale RAG benchmark of 4,409 QA pairs across 5 domains and 8 question types, with mock web and knowledge-graph search APIs and a correct/missing/hallucinated scoring scheme. Its question-type taxonomy (aggregation, comparison, multi-hop) raised the difficulty bar for RAG QA evaluation.
nodes.findings: State-of-the-art industry RAG systems achieve at most 63% hallucination-free accuracy, performing worst on dynamic facts, tail entities, and complex questions.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: the question-type taxonomy suggests harder query templates than a single position-question template, and the KG+text hybrid parallels dual retrieval channels.

nodes.label: GroUSE
nodes.summary: 144 unit tests probing whether judges detect 7 grounded-QA failure modes; RAGAS/DeepEval-style pipelines overlook important failures even with GPT-4; judge-judge correlation is a misleading validity proxy.
nodes.significance: Meta-evaluation of grounded-QA judges through 144 unit tests probing 7 failure modes, showing that judge-judge correlation is a misleading validity proxy and that adding an LLM judge is not automatically more valid than deterministic checks.
nodes.findings: RAGAS/DeepEval-style pipelines overlook important failure modes even with GPT-4 as judge; open judges correlate strongly with GPT-4 yet still fail the unit tests.

nodes.label: RAGChecker
nodes.summary: Claim-level entailment decomposition of answers and ground truths into diagnostic retriever metrics (claim recall, context precision) and generator metrics (faithfulness, noise sensitivity, hallucination).
nodes.significance: Claim-level entailment decomposition of answers and ground truths into diagnostic retriever metrics (claim recall, context precision) and generator metrics (faithfulness, noise sensitivity, hallucination), offering a middle ground between deterministic verification and holistic LLM judging.
nodes.findings: Reports significantly better correlation with human judgments than prior RAG evaluation metrics.

nodes.label: LLM-as-a-Judge (MT-Bench)
nodes.summary: Canonical LLM-judge paper: GPT-4 matches human preferences at >80% agreement (human-human level); documents position, verbosity, and self-enhancement bias with mitigations.
nodes.significance: Canonical paper establishing LLM-as-a-judge as an evaluation paradigm, showing GPT-4 can match human preferences at human-human agreement levels while documenting position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases with mitigations such as order swapping and reference-guided judging.
nodes.findings: A GPT-4 judge matches human preferences at over 80% agreement, the same level as human-human agreement.
nodes.limitations: Documents position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias in LLM judges, requiring explicit controls.

nodes.label: LLM evaluators favor their own generations
nodes.summary: GPT-4/Llama-2 recognize their own outputs out of the box; fine-tuning shows a linear link between self-recognition capability and self-preference strength: a causal recognition-to-preference route.
nodes.significance: Mechanistic study of self-preference in LLM evaluators showing the bias is driven by recognition of the generator's style rather than output quality, implying it cannot be removed by prompting and motivating judges from a different model family than the generator.
nodes.findings: GPT-4 and Llama-2 recognize their own outputs with non-trivial accuracy out of the box; fine-tuning reveals a linear correlation between self-recognition capability and self-preference strength, evidence of a causal recognition-to-preference link.

nodes.label: LLMs are not fair evaluators
nodes.summary: Pairwise verdicts hackable by response order alone: Vicuna-13B 'beats' ChatGPT on 66/80 queries purely via ordering; proposes balanced position calibration.
nodes.significance: Demonstrates that pairwise LLM-judge verdicts can be flipped by response order alone, establishing position bias as a first-order threat to LLM evaluation and introducing balanced position calibration (judging both orderings and aggregating).
nodes.findings: With ChatGPT as judge, Vicuna-13B 'beats' ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries purely through response ordering.

nodes.label: G-Eval
nodes.authors: Liu, Iter, Xu, Wang, Xu & Zhu
nodes.summary: CoT + form-filling GPT-4 evaluator with strong human correlation gains; the authors themselves flag its bias toward LLM-generated text over human-written text.
nodes.significance: Chain-of-thought, form-filling GPT-4 evaluator that substantially improved correlation with human judgments over prior NLG metrics, while documenting that even a well-designed rubric judge prefers LLM-generated text over human-written text.
nodes.findings: Reaches Spearman correlation of 0.514 with human judgments on SummEval, a large gain over prior metrics; it preferred GPT-3.5 summaries in cases where humans preferred human-written ones.
nodes.limitations: The authors themselves flag its bias toward LLM-generated text, making absolute rubric scores less trustworthy than human-anchored pairwise comparisons.

nodes.label: PoLL (Panel of LLM evaluators)
nodes.summary: A panel of small judges from disjoint model families outperforms a single GPT-4 judge in human correlation, mitigates intra-model bias, and is >7x cheaper.
nodes.significance: Proposes replacing a single large LLM judge with a panel of small judges drawn from disjoint model families, improving correlation with human judgments while mitigating intra-model bias and reducing cost.
nodes.findings: A panel of small judges from disjoint families outperforms a single GPT-4 judge in human correlation across 3 judge settings and 6 datasets, mitigates intra-model bias, and is more than 7x cheaper.
nodes.limitations: arXiv-only preprint; not confirmed as peer reviewed.

nodes.label: Self-preference bias mechanism
nodes.summary: Judges over-score low-perplexity (familiar) text relative to humans, independent of literal self-generation.
nodes.significance: Quantifies self-preference bias in LLM judges and identifies its mechanism: judges over-score low-perplexity (familiar) text relative to humans, independent of literal self-generation, which generalizes self-preference to same-family model outputs.
nodes.findings: GPT-4 shows significant self-preference; the effect is driven by low-perplexity familiarity with the text rather than by having literally generated it.

nodes.label: Preference Leakage
nodes.summary: Formalizes generator-judge relatedness (same model, distilled, same family) and shows systematic bias toward related models; contamination is harder to detect than position or verbosity bias.
nodes.significance: Formalizes generator-judge relatedness (same model, distilled/student, same model family) and shows systematic judge bias toward related models via a preference leakage score, establishing that same-family judging is contaminated by construction.
nodes.findings: Shows systematic bias toward related models across baselines and benchmarks; the contamination is harder to detect than position or verbosity bias.

nodes.label: JudgeBench
nodes.summary: On deliberately hard pairs where factual correctness decides the winner, strong judges including GPT-4o are barely above random (~50%).
nodes.significance: Meta-evaluation benchmark testing LLM judges on deliberately hard response pairs where factual correctness rather than style decides the winner, showing that preference-based judge benchmarks overstate judge competence on factuality.
nodes.findings: On pairs decided by factual correctness, strong judges including GPT-4o are barely above random (~50%).

nodes.label: AutoEval Done Right (PPI)
nodes.summary: PPI-family estimators combine LLM-judge labels with a small human-labeled set into unbiased comparisons, stretching effective human-sample size by up to ~50%.
nodes.significance: Applies prediction-powered inference to model evaluation, combining plentiful LLM-judge labels with a small human-labeled set to obtain unbiased comparisons and rankings with honest confidence intervals.
nodes.findings: PPI-family estimators increased effective human-sample size by up to ~50% in GPT-4 experiments.
nodes.limitations: arXiv-only preprint; venue not confirmed as peer reviewed.

nodes.label: Human NLG eval best practices
nodes.authors: van der Lee, Gatt, van Miltenburg, Wubben & Krahmer
nodes.summary: Field survey of human NLG evaluation: Likert dominance, minority IAA and significance reporting; recommends more raters, mandatory agreement statistics, full protocol documentation.
nodes.significance: Field survey and best-practice guideline for human evaluation of automatically generated text, documenting the dominance of Likert scales and minority reporting of agreement and significance, and recommending more raters, mandatory agreement statistics, and full protocol documentation.
nodes.findings: 5- and 7-point Likert scales dominate the field while inter-annotator agreement and significance testing are reported only by minorities of papers; field-typical NLG inter-annotator agreement sits around 0.3-0.5 or lower.

nodes.label: Twenty Years of Confusion
nodes.summary: 165 NLG papers use 200+ distinct, mostly undefined quality-criterion names; proposes standardized definitions and evaluation sheets.
nodes.significance: Documents two decades of terminological confusion in human NLG evaluation and proposes standardized criterion definitions and evaluation sheets; low agreement across many loosely defined Likert dimensions is a textbook symptom of criterion ambiguity rather than noisy raters.
nodes.findings: Across 165 NLG papers, over 200 distinct and mostly undefined quality-criterion names are in use.

nodes.label: With Little Power (Card et al.)
nodes.authors: Card, Henderson, Khandelwal, Jia, Mahowald & Jurafsky
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of NLP human evaluations: the modal design (3 annotators x 100 items) is underpowered unless the true effect exceeds ~0.2; recommends prospective power analysis and mixed-effects models.
nodes.significance: Meta-analysis of statistical power in NLP human evaluations showing that the field's modal study design is underpowered for typical effect sizes, and recommending prospective power analysis, mixed-effects models, and release of raw ratings.
nodes.findings: 69% of EMNLP 2019 human evaluations used at most 100 items; the modal design (3 annotators x 100 items) is underpowered unless the true effect exceeds ~0.2 on a [0,1] scale; small effects require 10+ raters on 100+ items.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: directly explains why a small expert study (few raters, tens of paired items) under multiple-testing correction yields null results as the statistically expected outcome.

nodes.label: Equivalence tests primer (TOST)
nodes.summary: Practical primer for two one-sided equivalence tests: pre-specify the smallest effect size of interest and reject both one-sided nulls to claim equivalence.
nodes.significance: Practical primer for equivalence testing via two one-sided tests (TOST): pre-specify the smallest effect size of interest and reject both one-sided nulls to make an affirmative equivalence claim, converting non-significant results into positive non-inferiority statements.
nodes.limitations: Equivalence testing requires larger samples than difference testing for the same effect bounds.

nodes.label: Best-Worst Scaling reliability
nodes.summary: At equal annotation budget, best-worst scaling is far more reliable than rating scales, which suffer scale-interpretation inconsistency and region bias.
nodes.significance: Shows that best-worst scaling is substantially more reliable than rating scales at equal annotation budget, identifying scale-interpretation inconsistency and scale-region bias as mechanisms behind ceiling effects and depressed agreement in Likert-style data.
nodes.findings: At the same annotation budget, best-worst scaling far exceeds rating scales on split-half reliability.

nodes.label: LLM relevance judgment perspectives
nodes.summary: Position paper defining the human-machine collaboration spectrum for relevance judgments, with cautions on prompt sensitivity and circularity.
nodes.significance: Position paper defining the human-machine collaboration spectrum for relevance judgments, from fully manual to fully automated, legitimizing pooling with LLM qrels plus small human validation as an endorsed mid-spectrum strategy while cautioning about prompt sensitivity and circularity.
nodes.findings: Pilot experiments with GPT-3.5 reached kappa of roughly 0.26-0.40 against TREC labels.

nodes.label: LLMs predict searcher preferences
nodes.summary: GPT-4 relevance labels reach kappa 0.64 vs NIST (best prompt), exceeding trained inter-assessor agreement (0.52); in Bing production since 2022 at ~1/20 crowd cost; kappa swings 0.2+ across paraphrases.
nodes.significance: Production-scale evidence that LLM relevance labels can match or exceed trained human inter-assessor agreement, establishing concrete acceptance thresholds for LLM assessors and prescribing the role of small gold sets for prompt selection and monitoring.
nodes.findings: GPT-4 reaches kappa 0.20-0.64 vs NIST depending on prompt (best 0.64), exceeding trained inter-assessor agreement (kappa 0.52); system-ranking consistency tau 0.77-0.86 over 110 runs; deployed in Bing production since late 2022 at roughly 1/20 crowd cost with +28% relative accuracy over typical crowd labels.
nodes.limitations: Kappa swings by 0.2 or more across prompt paraphrases, so a small gold set is needed to select and monitor the prompt.

nodes.label: UMBRELA
nodes.summary: Open reproduction of LLM relevance assessment with GPT-4o: modest per-label kappa (0.42-0.50 binarized) but near-perfect system-ranking correlation (Kendall tau 0.87-0.94); used for TREC 2024 RAG.
nodes.significance: Open reproduction of LLM relevance assessment with GPT-4o, showing that modest per-label agreement still yields near-perfect system-ranking correlation; adopted for the TREC 2024 RAG track assessments.
nodes.findings: On TREC DL 2019-23, kappa vs NIST is 0.31-0.37 on 4-grade labels (0.42-0.50 binarized), yet Kendall tau of system rankings (nDCG@10) reaches 0.87-0.94.
nodes.limitations: arXiv-only preprint with no proceedings entry found at verification time.

nodes.label: TREC 2024 RAG / AutoNuggetizer
nodes.authors: Pradeep, Thakur, Upadhyay, Campos, Craswell & Lin
nodes.summary: Revives nugget-based evaluation for RAG: LLM-drafted nuggets from pooled evidence, support labels per answer; run-level Kendall tau 0.783 automatic vs manual, noisier per topic.
nodes.significance: Revives nugget-based evaluation for RAG: an LLM drafts information nuggets from pooled evidence and assigns per-answer support labels, providing a scalable methodology for end-to-end answer completeness assessment.
nodes.findings: Over 21 topics and 45 runs, run-level Kendall tau between automatic and (mostly) manual evaluation is 0.783; per-topic tau is 0.518, reliable for ranking systems but noisy per topic.
nodes.limitations: Per-topic agreement is noisy (tau 0.518); published as a TREC track report rather than a peer-reviewed paper.

nodes.label: Voorhees 2000 (assessor variation)
nodes.summary: Absolute retrieval scores shift with the assessor, but relative system orderings are stable across assessors' qrels (Kendall tau ~0.94).
nodes.significance: Foundational demonstration that absolute retrieval scores shift with the assessor while relative system orderings remain stable across assessors' qrels, licensing comparative evaluation based on pooling and a single consistent assessor.
nodes.findings: Relative system orderings are stable across different assessors' qrels at Kendall tau of approximately 0.94, despite shifts in absolute scores.

nodes.label: Don't use LLMs for relevance judgments
nodes.summary: Position: LLM-authored truth data collapses retrieval and evaluation into one problem and sets that LLM as a performance ceiling; LLMs may assist but final judgments should stay human-grounded.
nodes.significance: Position paper arguing that LLM-authored relevance judgments collapse retrieval and evaluation into a single problem and set the judging LLM as a performance ceiling; LLMs may assist with drafting and prioritizing, but final judgments should remain human-grounded and LLM-derived collections should not be labeled ground truth.

nodes.label: LLM judgments can't replace humans
nodes.summary: Critique of LLM relevance assessment: circularity (LLM judges can favor systems built on similar LLMs), leaderboard correlation is insufficient validity evidence, prompt sensitivity.
nodes.significance: Critique of LLM-based relevance assessment highlighting circularity (LLM judges can favor systems built on similar LLMs), the insufficiency of leaderboard correlation as validity evidence, and prompt sensitivity.
